claims.text: The investigated nanoparticles are initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Rapid quenching produces a near-homogeneous solid solution.
Rapid quenching preserves a random atomic distribution with little short-range chemical order.
Annealing the nanoparticles increases their short-range chemical order.
Annealed and rapidly quenched particles can be compared under otherwise identical heating ramps.
Vacuum annealing, X-ray diffraction, and DSC under an inert atmosphere are applicable thermal-characterization methods for HEA particles.
The melting comparison can be monitored by in situ high-temperature TEM and XRD under high vacuum.
Enhanced short-range chemical order produces atomic clustering and local compositional fluctuations.
The local compositional fluctuations associated with chemical ordering lower local effective cohesive-energy barriers.
Lower local cohesive-energy barriers facilitate atomic mobility at lower temperatures.
The enhanced atomic mobility causes earlier surface disordering and initiates premelting at a lower temperature.
Annealed nanoparticles with enhanced short-range order will have a lower premelting onset temperature than rapidly quenched nanoparticles.
Annealed nanoparticles will exhibit more pronounced diffuse melting signatures in DSC and in situ imaging.
Rapidly quenched random-solid-solution particles have higher local cohesive energies and a higher effective melting barrier than annealed particles.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to particles approximately 10–20 nm in size.
The proposed relationship applies only when surface effects and particle coarsening are minimized.
Significant oxidation or agglomeration may dominate the thermal response and invalidate the proposed ordering-controlled regime.
A lack of a statistically significant reduction in premelting onset, or any discernible change in melting-transition characteristics, in the annealed particles would falsify the hypothesis.
